p.l: O Zeus, why do you talk to yourself alone, deep in thought,
Pacing about pale, with the complexion of a philosopher?
Confide in me, take me as counselor in your troubles,
And do not despise a servant's chatter!
Yea, father of ours, son of Cronus, highest of rulers,
I clasp your knees, gray-eyed goddess Tritogeneia!
Speak out, hide it not in your mind, so we too may know
What plan gnaws at you in heart and soul,
Or why you groan deeply and pallor has seized your cheeks!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
There is no word so dreadful to utter,
No suffering, no tragic calamity,
That I do not outdo in ten ἰαμβείοις ὑπερπαίω Text P (Vat. 76) D (Bodl. B 56); ἰαμβιοισιν P, ἰαμβείοισι D; ὑπερπαίδεκα D. ἦς οὐκ ἂν ἄραιτʼ (ἄροιτʼ) ἄχθος ἡ θεῶν φύσιε γ, NHA, edd. D has this line also, after the other.iambic lines!

sp.speaker: Athene
sp.p: Apollo! With what a prelude you begin your speech!

p.l: O most accursed earthly nurslings of the soil,
And you, Prometheus, what evils you have wrought me!

sp.speaker: Athene
sp.p: What is it? You will be speaking to a chorus of your own kin.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: O whirring flash of loud-roaring lightning, what τί Guyet: τί μοι MSS.wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Calm your wrath, Zeus, if I cannot act comedy or recite epic like these two, nor have swallowed all of Euripides whole so as to play tragedy opposite you!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Do you think I don't know the cause of your grief, whatever it is?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You know not—else loudly would you wail!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: I know the main point of what ails you—that it is a love affair! Still, I don't wail, out of habit, having already been insulted by you in this way many times. Likely you've found some Danaë or Semele or Europa again and are tormented by love, and now you're plotting to turn into a bull or satyr or gold and pour through the roof into your beloved's lap! For these symptoms—sighs, tears, and pallor—belong to nothing else but love.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Bless your soul, thinking our troubles have to do with love and such trifles!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Well, what else but that could possibly grieve you, being Zeus?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: The affairs of the gods are in direst straits, Hera, and—as the saying goes—stand on a razor's edge, whether we are still to be honored and receive our dues on earth or be utterly neglected and counted as nothing!

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: Has Earth bred some Giants again, or have the Titans broken their chains, overpowered their guards, and taken up arms against us once more?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Take heart—below, all is secure for the gods.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: What other terrible thing could there be, then? For if nothing like that is troubling you, I fail to see why you've turned into Polus or Aristodemus instead of Zeus!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Yesterday, Hera, Timocles the Stoic and Damis the Epicurean—I know not how the discussion started between them—debated about Providence in the presence of a large and distinguished audience, which is what upset me most. Damis claimed the gods don't even exist, let alone οὐδʼ . . . οὐχ ὅπως Harmon: . . . οὔθ' δλως MSS.oversee or govern human affairs, while good Timocles tried to fight on our side.
Then a huge crowd streamed in and the gathering reached no conclusion, so they broke up after agreeing to examine the rest another time; and now everyone is in suspense over which of the two will win and seem to speak more truly. Do you see the danger—how completely cornered our affairs are, staked on a single man? One of two things must happen: either we are cast aside, thought to be mere names, or we continue to be honored as before, if Timocles prevails in the debate.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: This truly is serious, Zeus—it was not for nothing that you played tragedy over it!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: And you thought I was worrying about some Danaë or Antiope in the middle of such a crisis! Well then, Hermes, Hera, and Athena, what should we do? Pitch in your own ideas too.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: For my part, I say we should call an assembly and refer the matter to the whole community.

sp.speaker: Hera
sp.p: I agree with him completely. παὐτὰ Κ Schwartz: ταῦτα MSB.

sp.speaker: Athene
sp.p: I think just the opposite, Father: don't throw heaven into uproar or make it obvious that you are rattled by the affair; instead, arrange privately for Timocles to win the argument and for Damis to leave the gathering laughed to scorn.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: No, Zeus—this won't stay secret since the philosophers' dispute is going to be held in public, and you'll look like a tyrant if you don't consult everyone on matters so important and common to all.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Make the proclamation at once, then, and let everyone attend—you are right.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Hear ye! Come to assembly, you gods! Don't delay—come all of you, gather round; we are going to hold an assembly on important business!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Do you make your proclamation so bare, plain, and prosaic, Hermes, especially when summoning them on the gravest matters?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: How do you want it done, then, Zeus?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: How do I want it? Give the proclamation dignity, I say, with verse and poetic grandeur, so they'll be more eager to come!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p:
Sure, but that's a job for epic poets and rhapsodes, Zeus, and I am not poetic in the least! I'll ruin the proclamation by stringing together lines too long or too short, and they'll laugh at the clumsiness of the verses—why, I see even Apollo getting laughed at for some of his oracles, even though their obscurity conceals
most of it so listeners don't have much leisure to scan the meter!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Then mix plenty of Homer's verses into your proclamation, Hermes—the ones οἷς Harmon ὡς MSS.he used to summon us; you're bound to remember them.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p:
Not very clearly or readily, but I'll try anyway:
Let no female deity θεὸς Word wanting in MSS. θεῶν ἔτι Hesdlam.... nor any male,
Nor any of the αὖ τῶν Mehler: αὐτῶν MSS.rivers remain away, save Oceanus,
Nor any of the nymphs; rather come all to the house of Zeus,
To assembly—all who feast on famous hecatombs,
And all of middle or lowest rank, or wholly
Nameless, who sit beside savorless altars!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Bravo, Hermes! Splendidly proclaimed! They are already gathering, so receive them and seat each according to his worth, depending on material or artistry: in the front row the golden ones, next after them the silver, then all the ivory ones, then the bronze or stone—and among these last let works of Phidias, Alcamenes, Myron, Euphranor, or similar masters have precedence, while this riffraff of
crude workmanship can crowd together somewhere in the back and merely fill out the assembly in silence.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: So it shall be, and they shall sit as is fitting. Still, it wouldn't hurt to know one thing: if one of them is solid gold weighing many talents, yet not finely crafted—completely amateurish and out of proportion—shall he sit ahead of the bronzes of Myron and Polyclitus and the marbles λιθίνων Bekker· τῶν λιθίνων MSS.of Phidias and Alcamenes, or should we consider artistry more honorable?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Artistry ought to come first, yet gold must be preferred nonetheless.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I understand—you're ordering me to seat them by wealth rather than merit, by property assessment! Step up to the front row, then, you golden ones!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: It looks as though only the barbarian gods will get front seats, Zeus! You can see what the Greek ones are like—graceful, handsome, and artfully shaped, yet all of stone or bronze, or the most expensive of them ivory with just a thin gleam of gold on the surface to tint and gild them, while underneath even they are wooden, sheltering whole colonies of mice living inside! Whereas Bendis here, Anubis over there, Attis beside him, Mithras, and Men are solid gold, heavy, and genuinely pricey!

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: How on earth is this fair, Hermes—for this dog-faced Egyptian to sit ahead of me, Poseidon?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Yes, Earth-shaker, but Lysippus made you out of bronze and poor, since the Corinthians had no gold back then; whereas this fellow is richer by whole mines! So you must put up with being pushed back and not get indignant if someone with a golden snout that size takes precedence over you.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Then take me too, Hermes, and seat me somewhere in the front rows—for I am "golden"!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not so far as I can see, Aphrodite! Unless I'm completely blear-eyed, you were quarried from white marble—Pentelic, I think—and then, when Praxiteles saw fit to turn you into Aphrodite, handed over to the Cnidians.

sp.speaker: Aphrodite
sp.p: Yet I can produce a trustworthy witness in Homer, who up and down his poems calls me "golden Aphrodite"!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: The same poet also called Apollo "rich in gold" and wealthy—yet right now you'll see him sitting somewhere among the middle class, stripped of his crown τε Fritzsche: γε MSS.by robbers and with the pegs of his lyre looted! So be glad you aren't sitting all the way back with the lowest class!

sp.speaker: Kolossos Rhodion
sp.p: Who would dare rival me, being Helios and of such immense size? Why, if the Rhodians hadn't seen fit to build me on so colossal and gigantic a scale, for the same outlay they could have made sixteen golden gods! So proportionally I ought to be considered more expensive—plus there is the artistry and precision of workmanship on such a scale.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: What should we do, Zeus? This one is hard for me to decide: if I look at his material, he's bronze, but if I calculate how many talents it cost to cast him, he'd rank above the top property class!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Why did he have to show up too, showing up everyone else's smallness and crowding the seating? Still, noble Rhodian, even if you are ever so much more worthy of honor than the golden ones, how could you sit in the front row unless everyone else stood up so you could sit alone, taking up the whole Pnyx with one buttock? So you'll do better attending the assembly standing up, leaning over the gathering.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Look, here's another tough problem! Both of these are bronze and of the same workmanship—each a work of Lysippus—and best of all, equal in birth as sons of Zeus: Dionysus here and Heracles. Which of them sits first? For they are quarreling, as you see.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: We are wasting time, Hermes, when we should have started the assembly long ago! For now let them sit mixed together wherever each pleases; another time an assembly will be granted to settle this, and then I'll decide what order of seating to establish for them.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Heracles, what an uproar they're making, shouting those usual everyday slogans: "Handouts! Where's the nectar? The ambrosia has run out! Where are the hecatombs? Share the sacrifices!θυσίας Text ΓΩΝ: some MSS. Repeat one or more of these Phrases."

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Quiet them down, Hermes, so they drop this nonsense and learn why they were called together.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Not all of them understand Greek, Zeus, and I'm no polyglot to make announcements intelligible to Scythians, Persians, Thracians, and Celts! Better, I think, to gesture with my hand and signal for silence.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Do so.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Bravo—you have made them quieter than sophists! Now it's time to address the assembly. See? They've been looking at you for a while, waiting to hear what you have to say.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Hermes, I won't hesitate to tell you, my son, what has come over me.
You know how bold and loud-voiced I always used to be in assemblies.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: I know—in fact I used to be terrified listening to you speak, especially when you threatened ἠπείλεις vulg.: ἂν ἠπείλεις γ; ἀπειλοίης β.to let down that golden chain and haul up earth and sea from their foundations, gods and all!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Well now, my child—I don't know whether it's the magnitude of the impending crisis or the sheer crowd present (for as you see, the assembly is packed with gods)—my mind is in a whirl, I'm trembling, and my tongue feels tied! And worst of all, I've forgotten the opening of the whole speech, which I had prepared so as to make the most impressive start before them!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: You've ruined everything, Zeus! They are suspicious of your silence and expect to hear some colossal disaster to explain why you're hesitating.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Would you like me to recite that Homeric opening to them, Hermes?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Which one?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: "Hearken to me, all ye gods and all ye goddesses!"

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Get out—you've parodied πεπαρώδηται du Soul: πεπαρῴνηται MSS.enough for us already at the start! Rather, if you agree, drop the clumsy verse and string together whichever of Demosthenes's speeches against Philip you like, changing a few words; that's how most orators make speeches nowadays anyway.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Good idea—a neat shortcut to rhetoric and a handy trick for those at a loss!

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Come on, start then!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: "I believe, fellow gods, that you would prefer it to great wealth if it were made clear to you what on earth this business is for which you have now been summoned. Since this is so, it is fitting that you listen eagerly to me as I speak. Now the present crisis, O gods, all but finds a voice and cries out that we must take firm hold of our affairs, whereas we seem to be thoroughly careless about them." And now—for Demosthenes is running out on me—I wish to explain to you clearly the exact events that alarmed me into calling this assembly.

Yesterday, as you know, when Mnesitheus the shipowner offered thank-offerings for his ship that nearly went down off Caphereus, we feasted at Piraeus—those of us whom Mnesitheus invited to the sacrifice. Afterward, following the libations, the rest of you went off in different directions as each pleased, while I—since it wasn't very late yet—went up to the
city to take an afternoon stroll in the Cerameicus, reflecting on Mnesitheus's stinginess: entertaining sixteen gods, he sacrificed only a single rooster, and an old, sniveling one at that, along with four lumps of frankincense so moldy they instantly went out on the coals without giving off even enough smoke for the tip of one's nose to smell—and this after promising whole hecatombs when his ship was already drifting toward the reef and inside the shoals!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: As I arrived at the Painted Porch thinking about this, I saw a huge crowd of people gathered, some inside the colonnade itself and many out in the open, with a couple of men sitting on benches shouting and straining their lungs. Guessing what it was—philosophers of the argumentative sort—I wanted to stop and hear what they were saying; and since I happened to be wrapped in one of my thick clouds, I reshaped myself into their style, pulled down my beard, and looked very much like a philosopher! Elbowing my way through the crowd, I went in without anyone knowing who I was, and found that rascal Damis the Epicurean and Timocles the Stoic, best of men, disputing fiercely. Timocles was already sweating and hoarse from shouting, while Damis, grinning sarcastically, was provoking Timocles all the more.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Their entire argument, it turned out, was about us! That accursed Damis was claiming that we neither exercise providence over mankind nor oversee what happens among them—which amounted to saying we do not exist at all,
for that was plainly the drift of his argument—and there were some who applauded him! The other one, Timocles, took our side, fought for us, grew indignant, and struggled in every way on our behalf, praising our care and explaining how we direct and arrange everything in proper order and harmony; and he too had some supporters. However, he was already exhausted and in bad voice, and the crowd was looking toward Damis; so, realizing the danger, I ordered night to pour down and break up the meeting. They dispersed after agreeing to return the next day and carry the inquiry to a finish; and as I walked along with the crowd on their way home, I overheard them praising Damis's points and already strongly favoring his side—though some refused to prejudge the opposite view and wanted to wait to see what Timocles would say tomorrow.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
That is why I have called you together—no trivial matter, gods, if you reflect that all our honor, glory, and revenue come from mankind. If they become convinced either that gods do not exist at all, or that existing we take no thought for them, we shall receive no sacrifices, no offerings, and no honors from earth, and we shall sit idly in heaven starving, deprived of those festivals, gatherings, games, sacrifices, all-night vigils, and processions! Since so much is at stake, I say all of us must devise some way to save the situation—so that Timocles wins and appears to speak more truly, while Damis is laughed down by the audience; for I don't have much confidence that Timocles will win on his
own unless help from us is added to his side. So make the lawful proclamation, Hermes, so they may rise and offer advice.

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: Hear ye! Silence! Keep order! Which of the full-fledged gods who has the right wishes to speak? What's this? Nobody stands up—you just sit quietly, stunned by the gravity of the news?

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: "May you all turn to water and earth!" As for me, if I were granted freedom of speech, I would have plenty to say, Zeus.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Speak up quite boldly, Momus—it is clear you will speak freely for our common good.

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p:
Then listen, gods, to what comes straight from the heart, as they say! I fully expected our affairs to come to this impasse and for many such sophists to spring up against us, getting the pretext for their boldness from ourselves. By Themis, it isn't right to be angry with Epicurus or his followers and intellectual heirs for holding such views about us. What else could one expect them to think, when they see such disorder in life—the good among them neglected, perishing in poverty, disease, and slavery,
while utter scoundrels and villains are honored, roll in wealth, and boss their betters around; temple-robbers going unpunished and escaping notice, while completely innocent people are sometimes impaled and beaten to death?

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: Naturally, seeing this, they conclude that we don't exist at all—especially when they hear oracles declaring that by crossing the Halys someone will destroy a great empire, without clarifying whether his own or his enemies'; and again, "O divine Salamis, thou shalt destroy the sons of women!"—since both Persians and Greeks, I think, were sons of women! And when they hear rhapsodes reciting that we fall in love, get wounded, get chained up, serve as slaves, quarrel, and have endless troubles—while still claiming to be blessed and immortal—what else can they do but rightly laugh at us and hold our affairs in contempt? Yet we get indignant if some mortals who aren't total fools expose all this and reject our providence, when we ought to be grateful if anyone still sacrifices to us despite our blunders!

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p:
And answer me truthfully here, Zeus—for we are alone and no mortal is present in the gathering except Heracles, Dionysus, Ganymede, and Asclepius, these illegally enrolled aliens— did you ever care enough
about people on earth to investigate which of them are wicked and which are good? You couldn't say so! Why, if Theseus hadn't wiped out the brigands as a sideline on his way from Troezen to Athens, for all you and your providence cared, nothing would have stopped Sciron, Pityocamptes, Cercyon, and the rest from living in luxury off the slaughter of travelers! And if Eurystheus, a just and provident man, hadn't investigated local troubles out of philanthropy and sent out this servant of his here—a hard-working fellow eager for labors—you, Zeus, would have cared little about the Hydra, the Stymphalian birds, the Thracian horses, or the insolence and drunken violence of the Centaurs!

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: To tell the truth, we sit here watching out for one thing only—whether anyone is sacrificing and sending up savory smoke from the altars—while everything else drifts downstream, swept along at random! So we are getting what we deserve now, and shall get worse as mankind gradually wakes up and discovers it does them no good to sacrifice to us and hold processions. Soon you'll see the Epicuruses, Metrodoruses, and Damises laughing at us while our advocates are defeated and silenced by them. Therefore it is up to you who brought things to this pass to stop and cure them. For Momus there is no great danger in going unhonored—I wasn't among the honored ones back when you were still flourishing and reaping the sacrifices anyway!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Let us leave this fellow to babble, gods—he is always harsh and fault-finding. As the admirable Demosthenes said, "To accuse, blame, and criticize is easy and within anyone's power; but to advise how the present situation may be improved—that is the mark of a truly sensible counselor," which I know well the rest of you will do even while he keeps quiet.

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: For the most part I live underwater, as you know, and govern my own realm in the deep, saving sailors, escorting ships, and calming the winds as far as I can. Still—since I care about affairs up here too—I say we should get this Damis out of the way before he comes to the debate, either with a thunderbolt or by some other means, lest he win the argument—for you say he is quite persuasive, Zeus. At the same time we'll show them how we deal with people who talk like that against us!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Are you joking, Poseidon, or have you completely forgotten that none of these things is in our power, and that the Fates spin out for each man whether he is to die by thunderbolt, sword, fever, or consumption? If the matter were in my power, do you think I would have let those temple-robbers walk out of Pisa unblasted the other day after shearing off two of my curls weighing six minas each? Or would you yourself have stood by at Geraestus while that fisherman from Oreus made off with your trident? Besides,
we'll look angry because we were stung by the affair, afraid of Damis's arguments, and therefore getting rid of the man without waiting for him to be tested against Timocles—so we'll simply look as if we won by default!

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Yet I thought I had hit on a neat shortcut to victory!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Get out—a tunny-brained idea, Poseidon, and thoroughly dense, to eliminate our opponent beforehand so he dies undefeated, leaving the argument still disputed and unsettled!

sp.speaker: Poseidon
sp.p: Then you lot come up with something better, if my plan is so "tunny-brained" to you!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: If we who are still young and beardless were permitted by law to address the assembly, perhaps I might say something useful for the deliberation.

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p:
The deliberation is on such grave matters, Apollo, that the floor is open to everyone regardless of age; it would be a fine joke if, facing supreme peril, we split hairs over legal eligibility! Besides, you are already a completely lawful speaker—long past youth, enrolled on the register of the Twelve, and practically of the council of Cronus's day! So don't act the boy with us; speak your mind boldly now without feeling
shy about addressing the assembly beardless, especially when you have such a heavily bearded, full-chinned son as Asclepius! Moreover, it would be especially fitting for you to display your wisdom now, unless you sit on Helicon philosophizing with the Muses for nothing.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: It isn't for you to grant permission, Momus, but for Zeus; if he bids me, perhaps I may say something not unmusical, worthy of my studies on Helicon.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Speak, my son—I grant you leave.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p:
This Timocles is a worthy, god-fearing man who has thoroughly mastered Stoic doctrines; consequently he associates with many young men as a teacher of wisdom and collects no small fees for it, being very persuasive when conversing privately with his pupils. In front of a crowd, however, he is terribly timid, with an untrained, half-barbarous delivery, so that he makes himself a laughingstock in public debates—unable to speak fluently, stammering and getting flustered, especially when in that state he tries to show off fine rhetoric! In intellect he is extraordinarily sharp and subtle, according to those who know Stoic philosophy best, but in speaking and expounding he ruins and muddles his points through weakness, failing to make his meaning clear, posing things like riddles, and giving even more obscure answers to questions—and the audience, not understanding,
laughs at him! Now one ought to speak clearly, I think, and take special care above all that one's listeners understand.

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: That much you spoke rightly, Apollo, in praising clear speakers—even if you don't quite practice it yourself in your oracles, being crooked and riddling and safely tossing most of them into no-man's-land so that listeners need another Pythian Apollo to interpret them! Still, what do you advise next? What remedy should we apply to Timocles's inability in speaking?

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: To provide him, if we possibly can, Momus, with an advocate—one of those clever speakers—who will express properly whatever thoughts Timocles supplies him.

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: That really is a beardless suggestion, still needing a tutor—to station an advocate at a philosophers' debate to interpret Timocles's thoughts to the audience, with Damis speaking in person on his own behalf while Timocles uses an actor, whispering his ideas privately into his ear, and the actor declaims without probably even understanding what he hears! Wouldn't that be a laughingstock to the crowd? No, let's think of some other way.

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p:
And you, my brilliant friend—since you claim to be a prophet too and have collected no small fees for it, even receiving gold bricks once—why don't you give us a timely display of your art by predicting which
of the sophists will win the debate? Surely you know the outcome, being a prophet!

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: How is it possible to do that, Momus, when we have neither tripod here, nor incense, nor a prophetic spring like Castalia?

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: See? You're dodging the test now that you're cornered!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Speak anyway, my son, and don't give this slanderer an excuse to malign and mock your art as resting on a tripod, water, and frankincense—as though without them you'd lose your skill.

sp.speaker: Apollon
sp.p: It would be better, Father, to do this at Delphi or Colophon, with all my usual apparatus at hand. Still, even stripped and unequipped like this, I'll try to foretell which of the two will win—only bear with me if my verses don't scan!

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: Just speak—and clearly, Apollo, not needing an advocate or interpreter themselves! After all, it isn't lamb and tortoise boiling together in Lydia right now; you know what the question is about.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
What on earth are you going to say, my son? Already these preliminaries to the oracle are terrifying—your color changing, eyes rolling, hair tossing,
Corybantic convulsions, everything utterly possessed, spine-chilling, and mystical!

p.l: Hearken to this oracle of prophetic Apollo
Concerning the chill strife which men have roused,
Shrill-voiced, armed with thick-packed words!
For back and forth in the battle's swaying cluck
They smite the topmost sterns of the dense plow-tail;
Yet when the crook-taloned vulture seizes the locust,
Then at last shall the rain-bringing crows caw;
Victory belongs to the mules, and the ass shall butt his swift offspring!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Why did you burst out laughing like that, Momus? Surely our present crisis is no laughing matter! Stop, you wretch—you'll choke from laughing!

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: How can I help it, Zeus, at an oracle so crystal clear and obvious?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Then interpret it for us right now—what does it say?

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p:
Completely obvious—we won't need a Themistocles! The oracle states right out in plain words
that this fellow is a charlatan, and you who believe him are pack-asses and mules, by Zeus, with no more brains than locusts!

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: Father, even though I am a resident alien here, I won't hesitate to say what I think: when they meet and start debating, if Timocles gets the upper hand, let's let the discussion go on in our favor; but if it turns out otherwise, then I myself, if you agree, will shake the Stoa itself and bring it crashing down on Damis, so the wretch stops insulting us!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Heracles, O Heracles, that is a boorish and dreadfully Boeotian idea—to destroy so many worthy men χρηστούε, K. Schwartz: not in MSS.along with one scoundrel, and the Painted Porch too, Marathon, Miltiades, Cynegirus, and all! If those collapsed too, how could the orators ever make speeches again, robbed of their grandest theme? Besides, while you were alive you might have been able to do something like that, but since becoming a god you've learned, I think, that the Fates alone have power over such things, while we have no share in them.

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: So even when I killed the lion or the Hydra, the Fates were doing it through me?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: And now if someone insults me by robbing my temple or overturning my statue, unless the Fates decreed it long ago, I won't crush him?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Not at all.

sp.speaker: Herakles
sp.p: Then listen to me speaking plainly, Zeus—for as the comic poet said, "I am a rustic who calls a spade a spade": if that's how things work with you, I'll bid a long farewell to honors, savory smoke, and sacrificial blood up here and go back down to Hades, where with my bow drawn even the ghosts of the beasts I slew will be afraid of me!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Bravo—"a witness from our own household," as they say! You'd have saved Damis the trouble by feeding him those very lines! ὑποβαλών Κ. Schwartz: ὑποβάλλων MSS.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Wait—who is this coming up in a hurry, made of bronze, finely proportioned and sculpted, with his hair tied back in the antique style? Why, it's your brother, Hermes—Hermes of the Agora, the one beside the Painted Porch! Look, he's covered in pitch from having casts taken of him every day by sculptors. Why have you come running to us, my boy?
Do you bring some fresh news from earth?

sp.speaker: Hermagoras
sp.p: Huge news, Zeus, requiring utmost haste!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Tell us at once if some other uprising against us has escaped our notice!

p.l: I chanced just now by bronze-workers
To be coated with pitch across chest and back;
A ridiculous breastplate around my body
Was molded and hung by imitative art,
Taking the whole impression of my bronze;
When I saw a crowd marching up, and two
Pale bawlers, prize-fighters of sophistry,
Damis and—

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Stop playing tragedy, good Hermagoras—I know who you mean! Just tell me this: has their battle been going on long?

sp.speaker: Hermagoras
sp.p: Not long; they were still in the skirmishing stage, slinging insults at each other from long range.

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: What else is left for us to do, ἕτι ποιεῖν λοιπόν Dindorf: ἕτι χρὴ ποιεῖν λοιπόν γ; χρὴ ποιεῖν N.gods, but lean over and listen to them? Let the Hours draw back the bolt at once, part the clouds, and throw wide the gates of heaven!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Heracles, what a crowd has turned up to
listen! I don't much like the look of Timocles himself, trembling and flustered—he's going to ruin everything today! It's obvious he won't even be able to stand up to Damis. Well, let's do the one thing we can—pray for him "silently to ourselves, lest Damis hear!"

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: What are you saying, you sacrilegious Damis—that the gods do not exist and do not exercise providence over mankind?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: No; first you answer me by what reasoning you were convinced they do exist.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Not at all—you answer, you villain!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Not at all—you!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: So far our champion is far better and louder at being rough! Bravo, Timocles, pour on the insults—that's where your strength lies, for in everything else he'll gag you and turn you as mute as a fish!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: By Athena, I will not answer you first!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p:
Ask your questions then, Timocles—you've won
that much by swearing an oath! Only without the insults, if you please.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Fair enough. Tell me then, you accursed wretch: do you not think the gods exercise providence?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Not at all.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: What do you say? All these things happen without providence?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Nor is the care of the universe directed by any god?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Everything drifts along at random?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: And you people listen to this and put up with it instead of stoning the sinner to death?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Why are you inciting the crowd against me, Timocles? Or who are you to get indignant on the gods' behalf, when they themselves aren't indignant? They've done nothing terrible to me despite listening all this while— if they are listening!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Oh, they are listening, Damis, they are listening—and in time they'll come after you!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: And when would they ever have leisure for me, having so much business, as you say, managing the infinite number of things in the universe? Why, they haven't even punished you yet for all your constant perjuries and the rest—not to force myself to hurl insults too against our agreement! Yet I fail to see what greater demonstration of their providence they could put on than crushing a wretch like you miserably! No, it is obvious they are away on a trip—across Oceanus perhaps, "among the blameless Ethiopians," for it's their habit to go there constantly for a feast, sometimes even uninvited!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: What can I say to such shamelessness, Damis?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Say what I have long been eager to hear from you, Timocles: how you came to believe that the gods exercise providence.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: First, the order of events convinced me—the sun always traveling the same path, the moon likewise, the seasons turning, plants growing, animals being born, and these very creatures so ingeniously constructed to feed, move, think, walk, build, cobble shoes, and all the rest: these seem to me to be the works of providence.

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p:
You are begging the very question at issue, Timocles! It is not yet clear whether each of these things is brought about by providence.
That events happen this way I would agree myself; yet it does not immediately follow that they happen through some forethought, for it is possible that having begun otherwise they now continue uniformly in the same way. You call their necessity "order," and then naturally you'll get indignant if someone doesn't follow you when you merely list and praise how things happen and imagine this proves each of them is arranged by providence! So, in the words of the comic poet: "That one is pretty shaky—give me another!"

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: For my part I don't think any further proof is needed beyond this. Still, I'll give one: answer me—do you think Homer was an excellent poet?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Very much so.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Well, I was convinced by him, as he makes clear the providence of the gods.

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p:
My brilliant friend, everyone will agree with you that Homer was a great poet, but no one will accept him or any other poet as a truthful witness on such matters! They don't care about truth, I think, but about charming their listeners; that is why they enchant us with meter, din myths into our ears,
and in short contrive everything for the sake of pleasure.

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Still, I'd gladly hear which passages of Homer convinced you most! Was it what he says about Zeus—how his daughter, brother, and wife plotted to tie him up, and if Thetis hadn't summoned Briareus, our noble Zeus would have been seized and put in chains? And in return, remembering Thetis's favor, he deceives Agamemnon by sending him a lying dream so that many of the Achaeans will die—you see, it was impossible for him to throw a thunderbolt and incinerate Agamemnon directly without looking like a swindler! Or did those passages draw you most to faith, where you hear that Diomedes wounded Aphrodite and then Ares himself at Athena's urging, and shortly afterward the gods themselves clashed and fought duels all mixed together, males and females, with Athena defeating Ares (already weakened, I suppose, by the wound he had received from Diomedes), and "Against Leto stood strong Hermes, bringer of luck"? Or did the story about Artemis strike you as convincing—how, being peevish, she got angry at not being invited to a feast by Oeneus, and so turned loose a monstrous boar of irresistible strength upon his country? Is it by telling tales like that that Homer convinced you?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
Goodness, gods! What a roar the crowd let out, applauding Damis! Our man looks completely at a
loss—he's sweating ἰδίει Κ. Schwartz: δέδιε MSS.and trembling and clearly about to throw away his shield, already looking around for a gap to slip through and run off!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: So you don't think Euripides says anything sound either, when he brings the gods themselves onto the stage and shows them saving the good heroes while crushing the wicked and the impious like you?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p:
Most noble of philosophers, Timocles, if the tragedians have convinced you by doing that, then one of two things must follow: either you believe Polus, Aristodemus, and Satyrus are gods at that moment, or you believe the masks of the gods themselves, their buskins, ankle-length tunics, cloaks, sleeves, padded bellies, and all the other props they use to give tragedy grandeur are gods—which is utterly ridiculous! Because when Euripides speaks in his own person, unconstrained by the needs of his plays, and states his own views, you hear him speaking freely:
Do you see this boundless ether up on high,
Holding the earth round about in its moist embrace?
Count this as Zeus, consider this to be god!
And again: "Zeus, whoever Zeus is—for I know not, save by report!"—and things like that.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: So all mankind and all nations have been deceived in believing in gods and holding festivals?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Bravo, Timocles, for reminding me of national customs—from which one can see best of all that the theory of gods has nothing firm about it! There is utter confusion, with different peoples worshiping different things: the Scythians sacrifice to a scimitar, the Thracians to Zamolxis (a runaway slave who came to them from Samos), the Phrygians to Mene, the Ethiopians to Day, the Cyllenians to Phales, the Assyrians to a dove, the Persians to fire, and the Egyptians to water. And while water is common to all Egyptians, locally the people of Memphis have the bull as a god, those of Pelusium an onion, others an ibis or a crocodile, others a baboon, a cat, or an ape; and even village by village, some have the right shoulder as a god, while those living across the way have the left; others half a head, others an earthenware cup or bowl! Isn't all this a laughingstock, good Timocles?

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: Didn't I tell you, gods, that all this would come out into the open and be closely examined?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You did, Momus, and your criticism was right; for my part I'll try to reform these things if we escape this present danger.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p:
Wait, you enemy of the gods—oracles and
predictions of the future: whose work would you call those, if not the gods' and their providence?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Keep quiet about oracles, my good sir, or I'll ask you which one of them you most care to mention! That one the Pythian delivered to the Lydian king, which was precisely two-edged and two-faced, like some of those double-sided Herms that look the same whichever way you turn? For why would Croesus crossing the Halys destroy Cyrus's empire any more than his own? Yet that Sardian fool bought that ambidextrous verse for no few talents!

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: The man is going through the very things I feared most, gods! Where is our handsome lyre-player now? Go down and answer him on this!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You are slitting our throats, Momus, criticizing us at the worst possible time!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Look what you are doing, you sinner Damis—you are practically overturning the very temples and altars of the gods with your talk!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Not all altars, Timocles—what harm comes from them if they are full of incense and sweet fragrance? Those of Artemis in Tauris, however, I would gladly see overturned from their foundations, on which the maiden delighted to feast on such offerings!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Where did this irresistible plague come from to pour over us? How ὡς vulg.: ὃς MSS.the man spares not a single deity, speaking freely like a festival reveller, and "seizes one after another, both the guilty and the innocent!"

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: Mind you, you'd find few innocent ones among us, Zeus—and pretty soon, as he goes on, the man will lay hands on one of the top brass too!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Then you don't even hear Zeus thundering, you god-fighter Damis?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Of course I hear thunder, Timocles! As for whether it is Zeus who thunders, you would know better, having come from up there among the gods; because people coming from Crete tell us a different story—that a tomb is shown there with a pillar standing over it declaring that Zeus can no longer thunder, having died long ago!

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: I knew a long time ago the man was going to say that! Wait—why have you turned pale on us, Zeus, with your teeth chattering from trembling? You ought to take heart and despise such little mortals!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p:
What are you saying, Momus—despise them? Don't you see how many are listening, how they are already won over
against us, and how Damis is leading them off tethered by the ears?

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: Well, Zeus, whenever you please, just let down your golden chain and haul them all up— "earth itself and sea itself along with them!"

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Tell me, you accursed wretch: have you ever sailed on a ship?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Many times, Timocles.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Then you were carried along either by the wind striking the sail and filling the canvas, or by the rowers, while one man stood at the helm steering and keeping the ship safe?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: So a ship could not sail without being steered, yet you think this entire universe drifts along without a helmsman or a commander?

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Bravo! Cleverly argued by Timocles, and with a strong ἰσχυρῷ Struve: ἰσχυρῶς MSS.analogy!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p:
Ah, most god-beloved Timocles, you would see that helmsman always planning what was helpful, preparing ahead of time, and giving orders to the sailors, and the ship had nothing useless
or senseless that wasn't altogether serviceable and necessary for their voyage. ?? μὴ . . . αὐτοῖς: text β.?? μὴ χρειῶδες ἦν αὐτοῖς γ.Whereas this helmsman of yours, whom you claim stands over this great ship, and his crew arrange nothing sensibly or according to merit: the forestay, as it happens, is stretched to the stern, and both sheets to the prow; the anchors are sometimes gold while the stern-ornament is lead; the underwater hull is painted in bright colors while the parts above water are ugly!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: And among the sailors themselves, you'll see the lazy, unskilled, cowardly fellow drawing double or triple pay, while the one ready to dive overboard, nimble at climbing the yardarm, and the only one who knows every useful task—him ἕκαστα μόνον, τοῦτον Jacobs: ἕκαστα, μόνον τοῦτον vulg.you'll see assigned to bail the bilge! It's the same among the passengers: some whipping-post sits in the front seat beside the helmsman being waited on, and another pervert, parricide, or temple-robber is showered with honors and occupies the best spots on the ship, while many decent people are crammed into the hold and trampled on by those who are genuinely their inferiors! Just think how Socrates, Aristides, and Phocion made the voyage—not even having enough barley-meal or room to stretch their legs on the bare planks beside the bilge—while Callias, Midias, and Sardanapallus enjoyed every luxury, living high and spitting down on those beneath them!

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p:
That is what goes on aboard your ship, most wise
Timocles—which is why shipwrecks are countless! If any helmsman were really standing watch and ordering everything, first he wouldn't be ignorant of which passengers are good and which are bad; next he would assign each his proper due according to merit—the better quarters up beside himself to the better men, and the lower deck to the worse—making some his messmates and counselors; and among the crew, the eager sailor would be appointed lookout at the prow or officer of the side or certainly promoted ahead of the rest, while the lazy slacker would get whacked over the head with a rope's end five times a day! So, my brilliant friend, this ship analogy of yours is in danger of capsizing for having drawn a bad helmsman! τετυχηκός vulg.: τετυχηκότος MSS.

sp.speaker: Momos
sp.p: Things are going downstream for Damis now—he's sailing full-sail toward victory!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: You judge rightly, Momus. Timocles can't think of a single strong point, just pumping out these hackneyed everyday arguments one after another, all easily overturned.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: Well then, since the ship analogy didn't seem very strong to you, listen now to my "sacred anchor," as they say—one you will never break by any device!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Whatever is he going to say?

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: See if this syllogism is sound, and if you can overturn it in any way: "If there are altars, then there are gods; now there are altars; therefore there are gods." What do you say to that?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: As soon as I've had my fill of laughing, I'll answer you!

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: You look as if you'll never stop laughing! Tell me anyway how what I said struck you as funny.

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Because you don't realize you've tied your anchor—sacred anchor though it is!—to a thin thread! By fastening the existence of gods to the existence of altars, you think you've secured a strong mooring from them! So, since you say you have nothing more sacred than this to offer, let's go home.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p: So you admit defeat by walking away first?

sp.speaker: Damis
sp.p: Yes, Timocles—because just like people being assaulted, you have taken sanctuary at the altars! So, by your sacred anchor, I am ready to make a truce with you right here at the altars, so we don't argue about this anymore.

sp.speaker: Timokles
sp.p:
Are you mocking me, you grave-robber, villain, scum, whipping-post, and offscouring? Don't we know who your father is, how your mother
was a prostitute, how you strangled your brother, commit adultery, and corrupt young boys, you utter glutton and shameless wretch? Don't run away until you leave with a beating from me too—I'll slit your throat right now with this potsherd, you utter abomination!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Damis is walking off laughing, gods, while the other follows him hurling abuse, unable to bear Damis's mockery—and he looks ready to hit him on the head with a tile! What are we to do after this?

sp.speaker: Hermes
sp.p: That comic poet seems to me to have put it well: "You haven't suffered any harm if you don't pretend you have." What's the huge disaster if a few men walk away convinced of this? Far πολλῳ Bekker: πολλοὶ MSS.more people believe the opposite—the great mass of Greeks and all the barbarians!

sp.speaker: Zeus
sp.p: Still, Hermes, Darius's remark about Zopyrus is very much to the point: I too would rather have this one Damis as my ally than possess ten thousand Babylons!
